## September 2023 House Judiciary oversight hearing

On Wednesday, September 20, 2023, Garland testified before the [[house-judiciary-committee|House Judiciary Committee]] in a roughly five-hour hearing in which Republican lawmakers lambasted his department's handling of criminal probes into [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]], [[hunter-biden|Hunter Biden]], the events of January 6 and other high-profile investigations.[12] Chairman [[jim-jordan|Jim Jordan]] opened by declaring "the fix is in" and repeatedly accused Garland of "slow walking" the Hunter Biden investigation to benefit President [[joe-biden|Joe Biden]].[12] Garland used his opening statement to argue that Republican efforts to target career officials were "dangerous" amid rising threats against public servants, saying "we will not be intimidated" and "we will not back down from defending our democracy."[12]

Under questioning from Rep. [[matt-gaetz|Matt Gaetz]] on the Biden family art-dealing arrangement, Garland confirmed that he had neither asked questions about nor investigated the matter.[12] Rep. [[kevin-kiley|Kevin Kiley]] pressed him on the inception of the [[doj-school-board-memo-2021|school board memo]], and Garland cited mainstream media coverage as the impetus while confirming that he had not spoken with [[fbi|FBI]] Director [[christopher-wray|Christopher Wray]] before issuing it.[12] [[ashe-in-america|Ashe in America]] wrote that Garland fumbled his words and appeared to perjure himself relative to prior statements, a charge Rep. [[thomas-massie|Thomas Massie]] made directly in a fiery exchange, and concluded that although the hearing was theater it was a reminder that Garland never reached the Supreme Court — a slight about which she argued he remained bitter.[12] The session is treated in detail at [[september-2023-garland-house-judiciary-hearing|September 2023 Garland House Judiciary Hearing]].[12]

## September 2023 shutdown cornering

With a shutdown looming just over a week away in late September 2023, McCarthy was described as having backed himself into a corner.[24] House Republicans were forced on Tuesday, September 19 to cancel a procedural vote on a 30-day stopgap [[continuing-resolution|continuing resolution]] intended to keep the government funded past September 30, and hours later five GOP lawmakers crossed the aisle to vote with Democrats to bring down the rule governing the [[pentagon|Pentagon]]'s spending bill.[24] Punchbowl News summarized the day as "a bad day for McCarthy and House Republicans."[24]

McCarthy's difficulty was that he needed votes from the [[house-freedom-caucus|Freedom Caucus]], whose members demanded the CR be split apart so that it would not fund what Rep. [[matt-gaetz|Matt Gaetz]] called "the election interference of [[jack-smith|Jack Smith]]."[24] Gaetz also wanted McCarthy to sign a subpoena to better investigate [[hunter-biden|Hunter Biden]]'s alleged "high crimes and misdemeanors," going so far as to draft the subpoena himself for the Speaker's signature.[24] The alternative — a Hail Mary appeal to Democrats for the votes needed to pass the CR — would likely have sealed McCarthy's fate given the standing threat by Gaetz and others to move to remove him from the speakership.[24]

[[burning-bright|Burning Bright]] argued that McCarthy was seen by disillusioned Democrats and Republicans alike as the embodiment of the [[uniparty|Uniparty]], and that Gaetz and the Freedom Caucus — widely read as executing [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]]'s will in the people's house — had him bent over a barrel on both the substance and the narrative of federal funding.[24] Caving to Democratic demands to fund the war in Ukraine would sharpen the line between America First and the Uniparty; caving to the Freedom Caucus would mark a shift in establishment deal-making toward sovereign nationalism and prove the movement had real power even without Trump in office.[24] Combined with the fact that Trump had de facto installed McCarthy as Speaker, Burning Bright framed the standoff as a deliberately constructed story.[24] See [[september-2023-government-shutdown-standoff|September 2023 Government Shutdown Standoff]].[24]

## Post-premiership advocacy for speech restrictions

After leaving office Ardern continued campaigning at the [[united-nations|United Nations]] for an international censorship framework, a call she had first advanced as prime minister in 2022.[2] In September 2023 legal scholar [[jonathan-turley|Jonathan Turley]] described her as one of the leading anti-free-speech figures in the world, noting that she continued to draw support from political and academic establishments and had by then taken up a position at Harvard.[2] In her latest intervention Ardern characterized free speech as a virtual weapon of war and demanded that the world join her in combating it as part of a broader campaign against "misinformation" and "disinformation" — views embraced, Turley wrote, not only by authoritarian governments but by Western governmental and academic elites.[2]

[[burning-bright|Burning Bright]] read the episode as evidence that the establishment and its media proxies feared not particular nationalist or sovereigntist figures — from [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] and [[robert-f-kennedy-jr|RFK Jr.]] to [[elon-musk|Elon Musk]] and [[vladimir-putin|Vladimir Putin]] — but what those figures represent: choice, which is born of sovereign will and expressed above all in the right, will and courage to ask questions.[2]

## We The People AZ v. Runbeck (2023)

In September 2023 Runbeck was the defendant in a public records suit brought by [[we-the-people-arizona-alliance|We The People Arizona Alliance]] after the company refused to comply with a lawful request for exterior and interior video of all loading dock locations showing items being delivered or picked up following Election Day.[4] The first hearing was held on Wednesday, September 20, 2023 and was covered live by [[badlands-media|Badlands Media]] on Rumble; the question before the court was whether Runbeck, acting as a government contractor, is subject to public records requests.[4] The Alliance sought two days of loading dock surveillance footage on the grounds that it was critical to ballot chain of custody, while attorneys for [[maricopa-county|Maricopa County]] and Runbeck argued the company was no different from a Staples or UPS Store and that its work product was no different from the toilet paper stocked in county bathrooms.[4] [[ashe-in-america|Ashe in America]] pointed to the sole-source nature of the county's Runbeck contract — which waives competitive bidding precisely because no other vendor can perform the service — as the smoking-gun refutation of that position, and reported that the judge committed to ruling expeditiously.[4] See [[we-the-people-az-v-runbeck|We The People AZ v. Runbeck]].[4]

## The 'kitchen sink' impasse

By Tuesday, September 19, 2023 the standoff had deteriorated sharply for Speaker [[kevin-mccarthy|Kevin McCarthy]].[2] House Republicans were forced to cancel a procedural vote on the 30-day stopgap measure, and hours later five GOP lawmakers crossed the aisle to vote with Democrats to bring down the rule for the [[pentagon|Pentagon]]'s spending bill.[2] Punchbowl News called it "a bad day for McCarthy and House Republicans," and [[zerohedge|ZeroHedge]] characterized a "kitchen sink" omnibus approach as the Speaker's only remaining path to avoid a shutdown — one that probably would not work.[2]

McCarthy needed votes from the [[house-freedom-caucus|Freedom Caucus]], whose members demanded the continuing resolution be spliced apart so that it would not fund what Rep. [[matt-gaetz|Matt Gaetz]] described as "the election interference of [[jack-smith|Jack Smith]]."[2] Gaetz additionally pressed McCarthy to sign a subpoena to investigate [[hunter-biden|Hunter Biden]]'s alleged "high crimes and misdemeanors," drafting the document himself.[2] McCarthy could alternatively pander to Democrats for the votes needed to pass the CR, but doing so would likely trigger the motion to vacate that Gaetz and others had threatened.[2]

## Uniparty framing

[[burning-bright|Burning Bright]] argued that McCarthy was widely perceived by disillusioned voters in both parties as the face of the [[uniparty|Uniparty]], while Gaetz and the Freedom Caucus were seen as executing [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]]'s will in the House.[2] Caving to Democratic demands to fund the war in Ukraine would deepen the divide between America First and the Uniparty; caving to the Freedom Caucus would signal a genuine shift in establishment deal-making toward sovereign nationalism and demonstrate the movement's power even with Trump out of office.[2] Because Trump had de facto installed McCarthy as Speaker, Burning Bright treated the whole confrontation as a narrative under construction.[2]

## Detroit counterprogramming and the second GOP debate (2023)

In September 2023 Trump planned to travel to Detroit on the day of the second Republican primary debate, injecting himself into the labor dispute between striking autoworkers and the nation's leading auto manufacturers.[296] The trip, which was to include a prime-time speech before current and former union members, marked the second consecutive primary debate he skipped in favor of his own counterprogramming; during the first debate in August he had sat for an interview with former Fox News host Tucker Carlson that posted online.[296] The decision to go to Michigan days after the [[united-auto-workers|United Auto Workers]] went on strike was read as evidence of how far Trump wanted to be seen looking past his primary rivals, and of the degree to which he and his political apparatus were already focused on a rematch with [[joe-biden|Joe Biden]].[296]

Rather than attend the [[second-gop-presidential-debate-2023|September 27 debate]] at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library and Museum in California, Trump intended to address more than 500 workers, with his campaign planning to fill the room with plumbers, pipe-fitters and electricians as well as autoworkers.[296] He had not directly addressed the striking workers' wage demands and had attacked union leadership, while more broadly casting himself on the side of autoworkers; his campaign also weighed a picket-line appearance, though an adviser called it unlikely given the logistical difficulties of his security protections.[296]

[[burning-bright|Burning Bright]] wrote that Trump never does anything by accident from a narrative perspective, arguing that he was demonstrating that the GOP debates — and by extension the conventional framing of the 2024 race — were beneath him, while eschewing legacy political posturing in favor of addressing national issues weighing on the collective mind.[296]

## September 2023 shutdown leverage

During the September 2023 funding fight, Gaetz was central to the [[house-freedom-caucus|Freedom Caucus]] bloc denying Speaker [[kevin-mccarthy|Kevin McCarthy]] the votes for a 30-day stopgap [[continuing-resolution|continuing resolution]].[11] He demanded the CR be spliced up so that it would not fund "the election interference of [[jack-smith|Jack Smith]]," and pressed McCarthy to sign a subpoena to investigate [[hunter-biden|Hunter Biden]]'s alleged "high crimes and misdemeanors" — going so far as to draft the subpoena himself and challenge the Speaker to sign it.[11] Gaetz's standing threat to move to remove McCarthy from the speakership meant that any attempt by the Speaker to pass the CR with Democratic votes would likely have cost him his post.[11] [[burning-bright|Burning Bright]] argued that Gaetz and the Freedom Caucus, seen as doing [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]]'s will in the people's house, had McCarthy — the perceived face of the [[uniparty|Uniparty]] — bent over a barrel on both the substance and the narrative of federal funding.[11]

## Questioning of Merrick Garland

At the [[september-2023-garland-house-judiciary-hearing|House Judiciary Committee hearing]] on September 20, 2023, Gaetz hammered Attorney General [[merrick-garland|Merrick Garland]] on the relationship between [[hunter-biden|Hunter Biden]] and [[joe-biden|Joe Biden]], with particular focus on the art-dealing scandal.[11] [[ashe-in-america|Ashe in America]] observed that the arrangement bore the classic earmarks of influence peddling and money laundering, yet Garland confirmed that he had neither asked questions about it nor investigated it.[11]

## Trump's counterprogramming

Ahead of the debate, reporting indicated that [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] planned to travel to Detroit on debate day to deliver a prime-time speech to more than 500 current and former union members, inserting himself into the dispute between striking autoworkers and the major auto manufacturers.[2] It was the second consecutive primary debate he skipped in favor of counterprogramming, following his online interview with Tucker Carlson during the first debate in August.[2] His campaign planned to fill the room with plumbers, pipe-fitters and electricians alongside autoworkers, and briefly considered a picket-line appearance that advisers called unlikely because of the logistical burden of his security protections.[2] Trump had not directly addressed the striking workers' wage demands and had attacked [[united-auto-workers|UAW]] leadership while casting himself broadly as their ally.[2] The venue for the debate he skipped was the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library and Museum, scheduled for September 27 in California.[2]

## September 2023 Garland oversight hearing

On Wednesday, September 20, 2023 the committee held a roughly five-hour oversight hearing with Attorney General [[merrick-garland|Merrick Garland]] in which Republican members attacked the [[department-of-justice|Justice Department]]'s handling of criminal probes into [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]], [[hunter-biden|Hunter Biden]], the events of January 6 and other high-profile investigations.[16] Chairman [[jim-jordan|Jim Jordan]] opened with the assertion that "the fix is in" even after what he called the face-saving indictment of Hunter Biden the previous week, and accused Garland of slow-walking that investigation.[16] Members including [[thomas-massie|Thomas Massie]], [[matt-gaetz|Matt Gaetz]] and [[kevin-kiley|Kevin Kiley]] generated viral exchanges over alleged perjury, the Biden family art-dealing arrangement and the origins of the [[doj-school-board-memo-2021|school board memo]] respectively.[16] Garland responded that Republican efforts to target career officials were "dangerous" and pledged that the department would not be intimidated.[16] See [[september-2023-garland-house-judiciary-hearing|September 2023 Garland House Judiciary Hearing]].[16]

## September 2023 meeting

At its meeting concluding September 20, 2023 the committee left rates unchanged in a target range of 5.25%–5.50%, a 22-year high, while issuing a more hawkish forecast than markets expected and simultaneously signaling a "soft landing" through higher growth projections.[2] The dot plot showed policymakers still anticipating one more hike in 2023, with the 2024 and 2025 median projections each rising by a half percentage point — a signal that rates would stay higher for longer.[2] Twelve of the nineteen policymakers expected one further hike that year while the remaining seven favored holding steady.[2] The median 2023 growth projection jumped to 2.1% from 1% in June, and officials cut their unemployment forecast, now expecting the jobless rate to peak at 4.1% rather than 4.5%.[2] The statement retained prior language about "the extent of additional policy firming that may be appropriate" and acknowledged that job gains had "slowed" while remaining "strong."[2] For fuller treatment see [[september-2023-fomc-meeting|September 2023 FOMC Meeting]].[2]

## September 2023 Garland hearing

As chairman of the [[house-judiciary-committee|House Judiciary Committee]], Jordan opened the committee's roughly five-hour oversight hearing with Attorney General [[merrick-garland|Merrick Garland]] on September 20, 2023 by declaring, "The fix is in."[22] He added that "even with the face-saving indictment of [[hunter-biden|Hunter Biden]] last week, everyone knows the fix is in," and accused Garland several times of "slow walking" the Hunter Biden investigation to benefit President [[joe-biden|Joe Biden]].[22] The hearing, covered at [[september-2023-garland-house-judiciary-hearing|September 2023 Garland House Judiciary Hearing]], also ranged over the department's handling of probes into [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] and the events of January 6.[22]
